statement: Default to traditional periodization (base, build, specific, taper) with a hard day-easy day weekly pattern; do not default to reverse periodization, which showed no advantage, and offer it only as a user-selected option with no benefit claimed.
appliesTo: All distances from 5 km to 100 miles; recreational and trained runners

statement: Offer block periodization (a 1-2 week concentrated intensity block followed by lower-intensity weeks) only as an opt-in, flagged-experimental mode for trained athletes; block lengths are design choices, not evidence-derived.
appliesTo: Trained or well-trained runners with limited weekly time; not novices

statement: Allow at least 48 h between a high-intensity session and the next hard session; 24-48 h after threshold-intensity work; no spacing needed after easy running. Use the 48 h end for novices or when readiness is low. Evidence reflects autonomic recovery only.
appliesTo: All runners; fitter athletes may use the shorter end

statement: Default to 1-2 quality sessions per week for recreational runners with all other running easy; elite descriptive data show roughly one threshold and one speed session weekly but do not establish this number for recreational or ultra runners.
appliesTo: Recreational runners; lower end for novices and ultra goals

statement: Use a mostly pyramidal intensity distribution in base and build; for 5-10 km goals allow a shift toward polarized work in the final specific phase; keep marathon and longer pyramidal (extrapolated beyond marathon).
value: pyramidal base/build; optional polarized final specific phase for 5-10 km
appliesTo: Distance runners; evidence from highly trained and elite runners

statement: No study compares 3:1 with 2:1 cycles. Default to 3 build weeks plus 1 recovery week, and use 2:1 for novices, older runners, post-injury returns or when a fatigue flag is active. These are conventions, not evidence-based values.
Reduce volume in a planned recovery week by about 20-30% while keeping some intensity and frequency; this magnitude is not empirically derived.
appliesTo: All runners; larger reduction when a fatigue flag is active

statement: Insert or extend an unplanned recovery week only when at least two independent signals agree (subjective fatigue/readiness decline, submaximal efficiency decline, sleep-efficiency drop), sustained over several days; a single signal only trims the next hard session. The sustain duration (default 7 days) is a design choice.
appliesTo: All runners with check-in and wearable data

statement: Collect a brief subjective check-in (fatigue, sleep, soreness, mood, readiness) as a first-class load-adjustment input, weighted at least equal to wearable-derived metrics; do not use mood questionnaires alone to separate overreaching from ordinary fatigue.

Track a standardized submaximal efficiency index (pace at fixed HR, or HR at fixed pace, plus HR recovery) and RPE across weeks; a sustained efficiency fall with rising RPE is an overreaching signal, while a rising index across weeks indicates positive adaptation. Thresholds must be athlete-relative and are not validated.
appliesTo: Runners with HR and pace data

statement: Never use resting HRV, post-exercise HRV or HR recovery alone to trigger or clear a recovery week or to declare good adaptation; they rise in both adaptation and overreaching. Do not use VO2max estimates for overreaching detection.
appliesTo: All runners using wearable HRV or HRR

statement: Treat a sustained drop of about 2 percentage points in wearable sleep efficiency versus the athlete's own baseline during a heavy block as one supporting overreaching signal, never a standalone trigger. Wearable accuracy was not assessed in the source.
appliesTo: Runners with wearable sleep data, during heavy blocks

statement: Cap non-recovery-week increases in weekly running distance at about 10% as a conservative default (design choice) and never exceed 30%; the only direct evidence is an exploratory, non-significant novice-runner association. Do not claim injury prevention, and do not use ACWR bands as hard rules; display ACWR only as a descriptive metric if at all.
appliesTo: Novice and recreational runners; ultra build phases not covered

statement: Compute weekly load, monotony (mean daily load / SD) and strain (load x monotony) from session RPE x duration, show them descriptively, and flag only when an athlete's own strain exceeds their personal historical range; keep daily load varied. No universal thresholds exist.
appliesTo: Runners logging session RPE or an HR-derived load proxy

statement: Use three states (normal, possible accumulated fatigue, persistent suppression); never output an OTS or NFOR diagnosis; allow a deliberate overreach block only when no flag is active; when suppression persists for about 4 weeks (design choice, borrowed from the OTS review criterion) or illness-like symptoms accompany it, prompt a medical review that mentions illness, under-fuelling and iron status.
